paper.title: Machine Unlearning of Federated Clusters
affiliations: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, USA
paper.one_liner: First exact-unlearning scheme for federated K-means: client-side K-means++ seeding that rarely needs retraining, plus Reed-Solomon-based secure sparse aggregation (SCMA).
paper.summary: This paper is the first to study machine unlearning for federated clustering (FC), where K-means data is spread across many clients and users can ask for their points to be deleted. The authors build a one-shot FC system, MUFC, designed so that deletions are cheap and exact. Each client runs only K-means++ seeding (no Lloyd iterations), snaps its K local centroids to a uniform grid, and records how many points each centroid represents in a sparse histogram vector of length B^d. SCMA, a new protocol, sums these vectors securely by treating them as Reed-Solomon 'errors' and sending 2KL masked syndromes. Communication is logarithmic in the vector length, and the server learns only the total histogram. The server regenerates points from the histogram and runs full K-means++. To delete points, a client keeps its seeding unless a deleted point was one of its chosen centroids. If one was, it resamples from the first affected centroid onward, and the paper proves the result is distributed exactly like retraining. The theory gives an O(log^2 K) approximation plus a quantization error term, and an expected removal time of O(RK^2 d) for random deletions (independent of n), versus O(nKd) for retraining. Across seven datasets the paper reports a ~84x average speed-up over retraining, and lower loss than K-FED/DC-KM on imbalanced data.
paper.problem: Federated clustering methods (e.g., K-FED, DC-k-means) either leak per-client centroid statistics to the server or are expensive, and none supports efficient data removal. With the right to be forgotten, clients may ask to delete some points (cross-silo) or leave completely (cross-device). Naive retraining of local and global clustering on every request is costly, and existing federated unlearning methods are empirical, with no guarantees on the unlearned model or on unlearning efficiency.
paper.core_idea: K-means++ seeding picks actual data points as centroids by sequential D^2 sampling. If none of the deleted points was picked, the seeding stays valid: conditioned on not having picked them, each choice has exactly the D^2-sampling probability on the reduced dataset, a rejection-sampling-style argument. Retraining is therefore needed only with probability about RK/n, and only from the first removed centroid onward. Clients send only quantized centroid counts, aggregated through a Reed-Solomon-syndrome-based secure sparse aggregation (SCMA). The server rebuilds a surrogate dataset from these counts and reclusters it, which is cheap because it depends only on K*L points.
paper.setting: federated unsupervised clustering (federated K-means), one-shot (single client-to-server round), cross-silo and cross-device removal
contributions: Introduces the problem of machine unlearning for federated clustering, and an end-to-end secure FC framework (MUFC) that supports simple exact unlearning.

Proposes a one-shot FC algorithm: client K-means++ seeding, then quantization and weighted counts, then server K-means++. It has an order-optimal O(log^2 K) approximation (plus quantization error) for the federated K-means objective and performs especially well on highly imbalanced clusters.

Proposes SCMA (secure compressed multiset aggregation), which uses Reed-Solomon codes with bin indices as evaluation points plus additive secret masks. The server recovers the exact sum of sparse vectors with per-client communication logarithmic in vector dimension (prior sparse secure aggregation is linear), and learns only the aggregate.

Proves that unlearning via K-means++ seeding is exact (probabilistic model equivalence), with expected removal time min{O(RK^2 d), O(nKd)} for random and min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(nKd)} for adversarial removals, independent of n, versus O(nKd) for retraining.

Compiles seven benchmark datasets for federated-cluster unlearning, including two new biomedical ones (TCGA cancer methylation, TMI gut microbiome), and reports ~84x average speed-up over complete retraining.
method_steps: Setup: scale all client data into the unit hypercube. Pick quantization step gamma (default 1/sqrt(n)), giving B = 1/gamma bins per dimension and B^d bins total. Pick a prime p >= max{n, B^d}. Offline, generate secure-aggregation masks z_i^(l), i in [2KL], with sum over clients of z_i^(l) = 0 mod p.

Client l (in parallel): run ONLY the K-means++ initialization (first centroid uniform, then D^2 sampling) on X^(l). This gives K centroids C^(l), which are real data points, plus local cluster sizes |C_k^(l)|. Store the centroids in their sampling order. Cost O(n^(l) K d).

Client l: uniformly quantize each local centroid to its grid bin index j. Build the sparse count vector q^(l) of length B^d with q_j^(l) = |C_k^(l)| for the bin holding c_k^(l), and 0 elsewhere (at most K nonzeros).

SCMA encode (client): send the 2KL masked syndromes S_i^(l) = (sum over nonzero j of q_j^(l) * j^(i-1) + z_i^(l)) mod p, for i = 1..2KL. The bin indices act as Reed-Solomon evaluation points and the nonzero entries as substitution errors.

SCMA decode (server): sum S_i^(l) over clients, which cancels the masks and leaves S_i = sum_j q_j j^(i-1). Berlekamp-Massey finds the locator polynomial g(x) = prod_{q_j != 0}(1 - j x). Factoring g over F_p (Kedlaya-Umans) gives the nonzero bin indices. Solving the 2KL-equation Vandermonde system gives the counts q_j. The server learns only q = sum_l q^(l).

Server data generation: for each nonzero bin j, sample q_j points uniformly at random inside the bin (default in experiments), or place the bin center with weight q_j (weighted K-means++, reduces problem size from n to KL). The result is the server dataset X_s.
Server: run full K-means++ (seeding + Lloyd's, up to T iterations) on X_s to get the global centroids C_s, at cost O(K^2 L T d). Clients keep C^(l). The server keeps X_s, q, and C_s.

Unlearning, single-client (cross-silo; R points X_R removed from client l): run Alg. 3. If no current centroid is in X_R, keep C^(l). Otherwise let i be the index just before the first removed centroid in sampling order, keep c_1..c_i, delete X_R, and resample centroids i+1..K by D^2 sampling on X' = X \ X_R. Recompute q^(l) only if client l reseeded. Other clients do nothing.
Unlearning, multi-client (cross-device; R clients leave entirely): set q^(l) = 0 for the departing clients. No client computation is needed.

Server update: re-run SCMA to get q'. If q' = q, keep C_s. Otherwise regenerate X_s' from q' and rerun full K-means++ at the server to get C_s', at cost O(K^2 L T d), or O((L-R) K^2 T d) for multi-client removal.

key_definitions.name: Centralized K-means objective
key_definitions.plain: Sum of squared distances from each point to its nearest chosen centroid.
key_definitions.formal: phi_c(X; C) = ||X - C||_F^2, where row i of C is argmin_{c_j in C} ||x_i - c_j||; optimum phi*_c(X)

key_definitions.name: Induced global clustering / federated K-means objective
key_definitions.plain: Each client point is assigned to the global server centroid that its LOCAL centroid is assigned to, not to the globally nearest centroid. The federated loss sums squared distances under this induced assignment.
key_definitions.formal: P_k = {x_i^(l) : x_i^(l) in C_j^(l), c_j^(l) in C_k^s}; phi_f(X; C_s) = sum_l ||X^(l) - C_s^(l)||_F^2

key_definitions.name: Exact unlearning (probabilistic model equivalence)
key_definitions.plain: The unlearned model has exactly the same output distribution as a model retrained from scratch without the removed point.
key_definitions.formal: for all C in M, x in X: P(U(A(X), X, x) = C) = P(A(X \ x) = C)

key_definitions.name: K-means++ initialization (D^2 sampling)
key_definitions.plain: Pick the first centroid uniformly at random. Pick each next centroid with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest centroid chosen so far.
key_definitions.formal: P(x) = d^2(x, C) / phi_c(X; C); E[phi] <= 8(ln K + 2) phi*

key_definitions.name: Random vs adversarial removal
key_definitions.plain: Random: every point is equally likely to be removed. Adversarial: a malicious user removes the points that matter most, e.g. boundary points or those contributing most to the objective. Experiments simulate this by removing the highest-cost point each round.

key_definitions.name: Cluster-size imbalance eps1 (Assumption 5.2)
key_definitions.plain: How much smaller the smallest optimal cluster is than a perfectly balanced cluster.
key_definitions.formal: eps1 = n / (K * s_min); eps1 = 1 means all clusters have size n/K

key_definitions.name: Outlier with parameter eps2 (Assumption 5.3)
key_definitions.plain: A point much farther from its nearest optimal centroid than the RMS radius of that cluster.
key_definitions.formal: ||x_i - c*_j|| > sqrt(eps2 * phi*_c(C*_j) / |C*_j|), where c*_j is the nearest optimal centroid, eps2 >= 1

key_definitions.name: Uniform quantization
key_definitions.plain: Round each coordinate to the nearest multiple of gamma. The grid cells are the 'bins'.
key_definitions.formal: y_hat = gamma * argmin_{j in Z} |y - gamma j|; B = 1/gamma bins per dim, B^d bins total

key_definitions.name: SCMA privacy criterion
key_definitions.plain: The server learns only the aggregated per-bin counts over all clients, not which client contributed points to which bin.
key_definitions.formal: server learns q = sum_l q^(l) only; masks z_i^(l) uniform on F_p with sum_l z_i^(l) = 0

key_definitions.name: Loss ratio
key_definitions.plain: Federated clustering loss divided by the (approximate) optimal centralized K-means loss. Lower is better; 1 is optimal.
key_definitions.formal: phi_f(X; C_s) / phi*_c(X), with phi*_c approximated by the best of several centralized K-means++ runs

theory.name: Theorem 4.1 (clustering quality of Alg. 1)
theory.statement_plain: With uniform quantization step gamma, the expected federated K-means loss of MUFC is at most O(log^2 K) times the optimal centralized loss plus a quantization error O(n d gamma^2 log K).
theory.assumptions: Data scaled to the unit hypercube; quantization uses the bin center as the reconstruction point (per-point distortion <= sqrt(d) gamma / 2); holds for any distribution of data across clients.
theory.significance: The O(log^2 K) factor is argued to be order-optimal for one-shot FC (two rounds of K-means++, each costing O(log K)). Choosing gamma = Theta(1/sqrt(n)) makes the quantization term independent of n. SCMA adds no distortion because it returns the exact sum.

theory.name: Lemma D.1 and remarks (no quantization, Alg. 5)
theory.statement_plain: Without quantization, E[phi_f] < O(log^2 K) * phi*_c(X). Restricted to non-outlier points, the bound is O(eps2 log K). If each client knows its true number of clusters K^(l) and runs K^(l)-means++, the bound is O(log K * log K'). In the extreme case where each client holds one whole cluster (L = K, K' = 1), E[phi_f] = 2 phi*_c, independent of K.
theory.assumptions: Uses the K-means++ guarantee at clients and server, and the triangle inequality ||a-b||^2 <= 2(||a-c||^2 + ||c-b||^2). Mirrors the distributed K-median result of Guha et al. (2003): an O(b) client and O(c) server approximation compose to O(bc).
theory.significance: Shows that data heterogeneity across clients can help FC quality.

theory.name: Lemma 5.1 (exactness of Alg. 3 unlearning)
theory.statement_plain: For any dataset X and removal set X_R, the centroids returned by Alg. 3 have exactly the same distribution as re-running K-means++ seeding on X' = X \ X_R, and E[phi_c(X'; C')] <= 8(ln K + 2) phi*_c(X').
theory.assumptions: Model = K-means++ initialization only (no Lloyd's iterations); seeding order is stored.
theory.significance: The proof is by induction over seeding rounds. Given c_i not in X_R, P(pick c_i from X | c_i not in X_R) = [d^2(c_i,C')/phi_c(X;C')] / [1 - sum_{x in X_R} d^2(x,C')/phi_c(X;C')] = d^2(c_i,C')/phi_c(X';C'), which is exactly the D^2 probability on X'. This conditional, rejection-sampling-style identity is the core tool. The paper states Alg. 4 (federated) is exact by the same argument; the server reruns from scratch whenever q changes.

theory.name: Lemma F.1 (retraining probability)
theory.statement_plain: If the probability that the dataset contains at least one outlier is O(1/n), a removal set of size R hits the K-means++ centroid set with probability < O(RK/n) for random removals and < O(RK^2 eps1 eps2 / n) for adversarial removals.
theory.assumptions: Assumptions 5.2 (imbalance eps1) and 5.3 (outlier definition eps2). Outliers are pessimistically assumed to always be chosen as centroids. The per-round bound is P(choose x_i as (k+1)-th centroid | C_k) <= 10 K eps1 eps2 / n, and a union bound over K rounds and R points is used.
theory.significance: Even a worst-case non-outlier point is unlikely to be a centroid, because the D^2 mass of any non-outlier is at most O(K eps1 eps2 / n) of the total.

theory.name: Theorem 5.4 (expected removal time)
theory.statement_plain: Alg. 3 removes R points in one request in expected time min{O(RK^2 d), O(nKd)} for random removals and min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(nKd)} for adversarial removals. Complete retraining costs O(nKd).
theory.assumptions: Same as Lemma F.1 (outlier probability <= O(1/n), Assumptions 5.2-5.3).
theory.significance: The expected unlearning cost does not depend on n. The proof gives E[time] <= O(nKd + RK) * O(RK/n) + O(RK) = O(RK^2 d). In the federated setting the client cost replaces n with n^(l), other clients do nothing, and the server costs at most O(K^2 L T d), or O((L-R) K^2 T d) for multi-client removal.

theory.name: SCMA communication and computation complexity (Sec. 4.3, App. C)
theory.statement_plain: Each client sends 2KL ceil(log p) <= max{2KL log n, 2KL d log B} + 1 bits, which is order-optimal given the lower bound max{O(KL log n), O(KL d log B)}. Client computation is O(K^2 L log(KL)) field operations. Server computation is max{O(K^2 L^2), O((KL)^1.5 log p + KL log^2 p)} (average case, because polynomial factorization is randomized).
theory.assumptions: Mask generation is done offline and its cost is not counted, following standard practice.
theory.significance: Communication is logarithmic in the vector length B^d, whereas prior sparse secure aggregation (Beguier et al. 2020; Ergun et al. 2021) is linear in the model dimension. Unlike sparsification approaches (Han et al. 2020), SCMA is exact.

theory.name: Unique decodability of SCMA (App. J)
theory.statement_plain: Two different aggregate vectors q and q' cannot produce the same 2KL syndromes S_i, so the server's decoding is unique.
theory.assumptions: At most KL nonzeros in q, so the difference has at most 2KL nonzeros; bin indices are distinct field elements.
theory.significance: The difference would satisfy B v = 0 with B a square Vandermonde matrix on distinct generators, which is invertible. This is a contradiction, so 2KL syndromes suffice.

theory.name: Deterministic low-complexity SCMA decoding (App. K)
theory.statement_plain: Replacing the prime p with a large non-prime p' >= max{K L B^(2dKL), n} + 1 avoids overflow. The server can then work over the reals, apply Berlekamp-Massey, and find the integer roots by bisection search on h(x) and h'(x). Worst-case complexity is O((MK)^3 d^2 log^c(MK) log B) for c < 2.
theory.assumptions: The symbol M in this bound is not defined in the text (probably L, the number of clients).
theory.significance: Removes reliance on randomized factorization over finite fields; deterministic poly(log p) factorization remains an open problem.

paper.complexity: Learning: client K-means++ seeding O(n^(l) K d). Client SCMA encoding O(K^2 L log(KL)) ops over F_p. Server SCMA decoding max{O(K^2 L^2), O((KL)^1.5 log p + KL log^2 p)} (average case). Server K-means++ + Lloyd's O(K^2 L T d). Communication per client 2KL ceil(log p) <= max{2KL log n, 2KL d log B} + 1 bits, logarithmic in the B^d-length vector and order-optimal; a naive secure sum of the full vector would cost B^d = gamma^-d entries, exponential in d. Unlearning: client expected cost min{O(RK^2 d), O(n^(l) K d)} (random) or min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(n^(l) K d)} (adversarial); other clients do nothing; server <= O(K^2 L T d) (single-client) or O((L-R) K^2 T d) (multi-client, no client computation). Retraining: O(nKd) per client plus the server. Compared with Q-k-means (Ginart et al. 2019), whose expected removal time is O(R^2 K^3 T^2 d^2.5 / eps), MUFC client unlearning needs only O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d) even for adversarial removals. Storage: clients keep their ordered seeding C^(l); the server keeps X_s, q, and C_s.

datasets: Gaussian (synthetic GMM; n=30000, d=10, K=10, equal clusters of 3000)
Celltype (Mouse Cell Atlas single-cell RNA, PCA to d=10; n=12009, K=4; cluster sizes 6506/2328/2201/974)
Postures (motion-capture hand postures; n=74975, d=15, K=5)
Covtype (forest cover type; n=15120, d=52, K=7)
FEMNIST (LEAF; 100 writers with >=350 points each; n=36725, d=784, K=62)
TCGA methylation (new; 4 cancer types; n=1904, d=57, K=4)
TMI gut microbiome (new; NIH Human Microbiome; n=1126, d=984, K=4; highly imbalanced 934/125/46/21)
models: K-means clustering (K-means++ seeding at clients; K-means++ + Lloyd's at server)
baselines: K-FED (Dennis et al., 2021), clustering quality only, since it does not support removal
DC-Kmeans / DC-KM (Ginart et al., 2019), adapted to FC with a computation tree of height 2 whose leaves are clients
Complete retraining (K-means++ locally and globally on each removal)
metrics: Accumulated removal time (s) over rounds of single-point removal
Single-round speed-up when no retraining is triggered
headline_results: Table 1 loss ratio (MUFC / K-FED / DC-KM): TMI 1.24/1.84/1.54; Celltype 1.14/1.72/1.46; Gaussian 1.25/1.25/1.02; TCGA 1.18/1.56/1.15; Postures 1.10/1.13/1.03; FEMNIST 1.20/1.21/1.18; Covtype 1.03/1.60/1.03. MUFC is best on the imbalanced TMI and Celltype; DC-KM is better on balanced Gaussian.
Single-round MUFC speed-up when the removed point is not a client centroid: TMI 151x, Celltype 1535x, Gaussian 2074x, TCGA 483x, Postures 613x, FEMNIST 53x, Covtype 267x.

Random removals, average speed-up over retraining (MUFC vs DC-KM, Fig. 3 legends): TMI 21x vs 5x; Celltype 44x vs 9x; Gaussian 30x vs 9x; TCGA 43x vs 2x; Postures 164x vs 7x; FEMNIST 6x vs 2x; Covtype 27x vs 4x. The text claims an ~84x average across the seven datasets; the arithmetic mean of these legend values is only ~48x, and it is unclear how 84x was computed.
Adversarial removals (MUFC vs DC-KM): TMI 9x vs 4x; Celltype 13x vs 8x; TCGA 51x vs 2x; Postures 224x vs 6x; Covtype 16x vs 4x (Figs. 3e, 4e-h).

Batch removals (App. M.5): TCGA 10 points/request 10x vs 2x and 30 points/request 4x vs 2x; Postures 10 points/request 18x vs 6x and 30 points/request 8x vs 5x. The speed-up shrinks as batch size grows.
The loss ratio stays nearly constant over 200-500 rounds of unlearning for both random and adversarial removals.
With full client K-means++ (Table 2), MUFC's loss ratio is best on all datasets: 1.05, 1.03, 1.02, 1.02, 1.02, 1.12, 1.02. Unlearning then costs about as much as DC-KM.
Non-iid data (K' < K) lowers the loss ratio (Fig. 3a). gamma has little effect on Gaussian data but strongly affects TMI, where the loss ratio explodes for large gamma (Fig. 3b,c).

limitations: Clients run only K-means++ seeding, not Lloyd's iterations, to keep unlearning cheap. Running full client K-means++ improves the loss but triggers retraining far more often (Table 2 vs Table 1).
Server-side unlearning is plain retraining: any change in q forces regeneration of X_s and a full K-means++ + Lloyd's rerun, O(K^2 L T d).

The removal-time guarantees need an outlier assumption (probability of any outlier <= O(1/n)) and depend on the imbalance eps1 and outlier parameter eps2. Outliers are almost always chosen as seeds and so force retraining.
Batch and adversarial removals reduce the gains (the union bound grows with R, and speed-ups shrink to 4-8x at 30 points per request).

The privacy notion is informal. The authors note there is no formal secrecy definition for FC, there is no differential privacy, and the server still learns the aggregated histogram of quantized centroid locations and counts. Leakage from comparing q and q' before and after unlearning is not analyzed (my observation).
Assumes a unique optimal clustering and no identical data points across clients. Data must be scaled into the unit hypercube, and the quantization error grows with d (O(n d gamma^2 log K)).

SCMA's efficient decoding is average-case, relying on randomized polynomial factorization over F_p. The deterministic variant needs an exponentially large modulus p'. Client dropouts and mask generation (done offline) are not treated.

Exactness of the federated Alg. 4 is asserted ('same as Lemma 5.1') rather than proved separately. Multi-client removal still requires a new SCMA round involving the remaining clients (my observation).
The headline 84x average speed-up cannot be reproduced from the per-dataset legends in Fig. 3 (mean ~48x) (my observation).
Only exact K-means (no other clustering objectives) is studied, and there is no conclusion or future-work section.
future_work: Not stated explicitly; the paper has no conclusion or future-work section.
Implied: a deterministic poly(log p) polynomial factorization over finite fields for SCMA decoding (stated as an open problem in App. K).
Implied: a formal secrecy or privacy definition for federated clustering (App. A notes none exists).
Implied: applying SCMA to other sparse secure FL aggregation problems ('as well as more general problems').
paper.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: MUFC shows a reusable design pattern for efficient exact unlearning: build the model from actual data points chosen by sequential randomized sampling. A deletion then matters only if the deleted point was selected, and when it was, you resample only from that step onward. The conditional-probability (rejection-sampling-style) proof of Lemma 5.1 is a compact tool that could transfer to coresets, prototype or exemplar selection, and other sampling-based learners. Expected cost scales with the probability that a point is 'used' (about K/n), not with n. It contrasts with Ginart et al.'s Q-k-means, which relies on stability of quantized centroids under small perturbations, and with SISA-style sharding; together these give three distinct routes to exact unlearning. Pitfalls to note: any Lloyd-style iterative refinement breaks the cheap path, the server still retrains fully, outliers and batch deletions erode the gains, and the 84x claim does not match the figure legends. For federated settings, SCMA is a practical tool: it delivers an exact secure aggregate of sparse updates at communication cost logarithmic in dimension.
open_questions: Make the server side incremental: apply the Alg. 3 seeding trick to the server's K-means++ on X_s, or bound how often Lloyd's output changes, instead of rerunning from scratch whenever q changes.

Extend exact unlearning to clients that run Lloyd's iterations, e.g. by combining MUFC seeding with Ginart et al.'s quantized-centroid stability (Q-k-means), and analyze the combined removal-time bound.

Formalize privacy for FC unlearning: quantify what the server learns from the difference q - q' between pre- and post-deletion aggregates, and add differential-privacy noise to SCMA while keeping exactness or certified unlearning.

Give tighter bounds for batch and sequential deletions (amortized cost over many requests) and design outlier-robust seeding (e.g., k-means-- or trimming) that keeps both exactness and low retraining probability.

Unlearning for multi-shot federated clustering (MFC) or fair/personalized FC (FFC): can the 'retrain only if a selected representative is removed' principle extend to multi-round or fairness-constrained clustering?
Generalize SCMA plus seeding-based unlearning to other unsupervised objectives (k-median, GMMs, spectral clustering) and empirically evaluate client dropout and mask regeneration during unlearning.

nodes.label: Machine Unlearning
nodes.description: Removing the influence of specific training data from a trained model, ideally more cheaply than retraining from scratch.

nodes.label: Exact Unlearning
nodes.description: Unlearning whose output model has exactly the same distribution as a model retrained from scratch without the deleted data.

nodes.label: Approximate Unlearning
nodes.description: Unlearning where the unlearned model only needs to be close (within a bounded difference, often DP-style) to the retrained model.

nodes.label: Right to be Forgotten
nodes.description: Legal right (GDPR, CCPA, CPPA) of individuals to have their personal data erased by organizations that hold it.

nodes.label: Data Privacy
nodes.description: Protecting individuals' data from being revealed or inferred by other parties, including model trainers and servers.

nodes.label: Federated Learning
nodes.description: Distributed learning where clients keep data on their devices and only send model updates or summaries to a central server.

nodes.label: Federated Unlearning
nodes.description: Machine unlearning in federated learning systems, where removal requests arise at clients and the global model must forget their data.

nodes.label: Clustering
nodes.description: Unsupervised grouping of data points so that points in the same group are similar.

nodes.label: K-means Clustering
nodes.description: Clustering objective that picks K centroids minimizing the sum of squared distances from points to their nearest centroid; NP-hard even for K=2.

nodes.label: Federated Clustering
nodes.description: Clustering data distributed across clients without centralizing it; the server learns global centroids from client summaries.

nodes.label: One-shot Federated Clustering
nodes.description: Federated clustering with a single round of client-to-server communication: clients cluster locally once and the server clusters the summaries.

nodes.label: Secure Aggregation
nodes.description: Cryptographic protocols that let a server compute the sum of client vectors without learning any individual client's vector.

nodes.label: Sparse Secure Aggregation
nodes.description: Secure aggregation specialized to high-dimensional but sparse client vectors, aiming to reduce communication below the full dimension.

nodes.label: K-means++
nodes.description: Randomized seeding for K-means that picks the first centroid uniformly and each next one by D^2 sampling (probability proportional to squared distance to the nearest chosen centroid), usually followed by Lloyd's iterations.

nodes.label: Lloyd's Algorithm
nodes.description: Iterative K-means heuristic that alternates assigning points to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids as cluster means.

nodes.label: Weighted K-means++
nodes.description: K-means++ in which each point carries a positive weight used in both D^2 sampling probabilities and centroid averaging; equivalent to point multiplicities.

nodes.label: Retrain from Scratch
nodes.description: Naive exact unlearning by retraining the model on the remaining data after every deletion request.

nodes.label: Secret Sharing / Additive Masking
nodes.description: Splitting or masking secrets with random values (e.g., masks that sum to zero) so that only aggregates can be recovered.

nodes.label: Quantization
nodes.description: Mapping continuous values to a discrete grid of bins; here uniform per-dimension rounding with step gamma.

nodes.label: Divide-and-Conquer Clustering
nodes.description: Cluster data subsets separately, then cluster the resulting representatives (e.g., Guha et al. 2003); approximation factors multiply across levels.

nodes.label: Reed-Solomon Coding
nodes.description: Polynomial-evaluation error-correcting codes over finite fields; syndromes of a sparse error pattern let a decoder locate and recover up to t errors from 2t syndromes.

nodes.label: Berlekamp-Massey Algorithm
nodes.description: Algorithm that finds the shortest linear recurrence (error-locator polynomial) generating a sequence; used to decode BCH/Reed-Solomon codes from syndromes.

nodes.label: MUFC (Machine Unlearning of Federated Clusters)
nodes.description: One-shot secure federated K-means framework: client K-means++ seeding, quantized centroid counts, SCMA secure aggregation, and server K-means++, with exact unlearning that reseeds a client only if a removed point was one of its centroids.

nodes.label: SCMA (Secure Compressed Multiset Aggregation)
nodes.description: Secure aggregation for sparse count vectors: clients send 2KL masked Reed-Solomon syndromes with bin indices as evaluation points, and the server recovers the exact summed multiset via Berlekamp-Massey, polynomial factorization, and a Vandermonde solve.

nodes.label: Unlearning via K-means++ Initialization
nodes.description: Exact unlearning for K-means++ seeding: keep the seeding if no removed point is a centroid; otherwise keep the centroids chosen before the first removed one and resample the rest by D^2 sampling on the remaining data.

nodes.label: Server Data Generation from Quantized Counts
nodes.description: Rebuilding a surrogate dataset at the server by sampling q_j points uniformly inside each nonzero quantization bin, or using the bin center with weight q_j.

nodes.label: K-FED
nodes.description: One-shot federated clustering (Dennis et al., 2021) where clients run K-means locally and send their exact centroids to the server for clustering; exploits client heterogeneity.

nodes.label: DC-k-means (DC-KM)
nodes.description: Divide-and-conquer K-means from Ginart et al. (2019) that clusters data subsets in a tree and supports deletion by retraining only the affected leaves and path.

nodes.label: Q-k-means (Quantized K-means)
nodes.description: Deletion-efficient K-means from Ginart et al. (2019) that quantizes centroids after each Lloyd iteration, so removing a few points rarely changes the quantized centroids.

nodes.label: Unlearning Cost
nodes.description: Computational (and communication) expense of processing deletion requests, often dominated by retraining.

nodes.label: Communication Cost
nodes.description: Number of bits clients and servers must exchange in distributed or federated protocols.

nodes.label: Data Heterogeneity (non-IID)
nodes.description: Clients hold differently distributed data, e.g. each client covers only some of the global clusters.

nodes.label: Privacy Leakage
nodes.description: Unintended disclosure of client data or statistics through shared models or updates, e.g. via model inversion.

nodes.label: Privacy-Accuracy-Efficiency Trilemma
nodes.description: The tension in distributed learning between protecting data privacy, achieving good model performance, and keeping communication and computation costs low.

nodes.label: Adversarial Removal Requests
nodes.description: Deletion requests chosen maliciously to target points critical to the model (e.g., boundary or high-loss points), forcing expensive retraining.

nodes.label: Outliers
nodes.description: Points far from their cluster center relative to the cluster's typical radius; D^2 seeding tends to select them as centroids.

nodes.label: Cluster Size Imbalance
nodes.description: Clusters of very different sizes, which hurt methods that weight all client centroids equally and affect removal-time bounds.

nodes.label: Unlearning Guarantee
nodes.description: A formal statement that an unlearning procedure removes the influence of deleted data (exactly or approximately).

nodes.label: Deletion Efficiency
nodes.description: Formal bounds on the (expected or amortized) time to process deletion requests relative to retraining.

nodes.label: Approximation Guarantee
nodes.description: A bound showing that an algorithm's objective value is within a factor (plus additive terms) of the optimum.

nodes.label: Federated K-means Objective
nodes.description: K-means loss in which each client point is charged to the global centroid that its local centroid maps to (the induced global clustering), rather than to its nearest global centroid.

nodes.label: K-means++ O(log K) Approximation
nodes.description: Arthur and Vassilvitskii (2007; cited as 2006): K-means++ seeding gives expected cost at most 8(ln K + 2) times the optimal K-means cost.

nodes.label: MUFC Clustering Bound (Thm 4.1)
nodes.description: E[phi_f(X; C_s)] < O(log^2 K) * phi*_c(X) + O(n d gamma^2 log K) for MUFC with quantization step gamma.

nodes.label: Exactness of K-means++ Seeding Unlearning (Lemma 5.1)
nodes.description: Alg. 3's output has the same distribution as K-means++ seeding rerun on the remaining data, and retains the 8(ln K + 2) approximation.

nodes.label: Retraining Probability Bound (Lemma F.1)
nodes.description: The probability that removed points hit the seeding centroids is < O(RK/n) for random and < O(RK^2 eps1 eps2 / n) for adversarial removals.

nodes.label: MUFC Expected Removal Time (Thm 5.4)
nodes.description: Expected unlearning time min{O(RK^2 d), O(nKd)} for random and min{O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d), O(nKd)} for adversarial removals, independent of n.

nodes.label: SCMA Logarithmic Communication Bound
nodes.description: Each client sends 2KL ceil(log p) <= max{2KL log n, 2KL d log B} + 1 bits, logarithmic in the B^d vector length and order-optimal.

nodes.label: SCMA Unique Decodability (App. J)
nodes.description: 2KL power-sum syndromes uniquely determine a vector with at most KL nonzeros, because square Vandermonde matrices with distinct generators are invertible.

nodes.label: K-means Cost
nodes.description: Sum of squared distances from points to their assigned centroids.

nodes.label: Loss Ratio
nodes.description: Ratio of a method's clustering loss to the (approximate) optimal centralized K-means loss; 1 is optimal.

nodes.label: Unlearning Time
nodes.description: Wall-clock time to process deletion requests, often reported as accumulated time over a sequence of removals.

nodes.label: Speed-up
nodes.description: Ratio of retraining time to unlearning time.

nodes.label: Gaussian (synthetic GMM)
nodes.description: Synthetic data drawn from a mixture of spherical Gaussians with known clusters.

nodes.label: Celltype (Mouse Cell Atlas scRNA)
nodes.description: Single-cell RNA-seq profiles of four mouse cell types, reduced by PCA; imbalanced clusters.

nodes.label: Postures
nodes.description: Motion-capture marker data of 12 users performing five hand postures (UCI MoCap hand postures).

nodes.label: Covtype
nodes.description: Forest cover type data with cartographic variables (USFS/USGS), seven classes.

nodes.label: FEMNIST
nodes.description: Federated Extended MNIST from the LEAF benchmark: handwritten digits and letters partitioned by writer.

nodes.label: TCGA Methylation
nodes.description: DNA methylation microarray beta values from The Cancer Genome Atlas, here for four cancer types at 57 promoter sites.

nodes.label: TMI Gut Microbiome
nodes.description: Human gut microbiome abundance profiles from the NIH Human Microbiome Project, roughly grouped by gender and age; highly imbalanced.

edges.note: Proposes the end-to-end secure one-shot FC framework with built-in exact unlearning.
Proposes SCMA for securely summing sparse client count vectors with logarithmic communication.
Proposes exact unlearning that reruns K-means++ seeding only from the first removed centroid onward.
Introduces, for the first time, machine unlearning for federated clustering.
edges.evidence: Abstract: 'We introduce, for the first time, the problem of machine unlearning for FC'

edges.note: Designs a new FC algorithm with privacy and low communication cost.
GDPR/CCPA/CPPA removal rights and medical data (UK Biobank) deletions motivate the work.
Aims to avoid complete local and global retraining for every removal request.
Positions MUFC as jointly addressing privacy, accuracy and efficiency while enabling unlearning.
Evaluates FC under the induced-global-clustering objective phi_f (Def. 3.1), following Dennis et al.
Proves the O(log^2 K) plus quantization error bound for Alg. 1.
Proves Alg. 3 is exact unlearning by induction over seeding rounds.
Bounds the probability that removed points are seeding centroids.
Proves an expected removal time independent of n for random and adversarial removals.
Shows per-client communication is logarithmic in vector dimension and order-optimal.
Proves the aggregated syndromes uniquely determine q via Vandermonde invertibility.
K-FED is the clustering-quality baseline; it is excluded from unlearning comparisons because it does not support removal.
Adapts Ginart et al.'s DC-Kmeans (tree height 2, leaves = clients) as the unlearning baseline.
Complete local and global K-means++ retraining is the reference for speed-ups.
Appendix G contrasts Alg. 3 with Q-k-means in intuition and removal time (O(R^2K^3T^2d^2.5/eps) vs O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d)).
Balanced synthetic data (n=30000, K=10), where DC-KM beats MUFC on loss.
Imbalanced scRNA data where MUFC has the best loss ratio (1.14) and a 44x random-removal speed-up.
Largest dataset (n=74975); 164x random-removal speed-up.
Forest cover data; MUFC loss 1.03 vs K-FED 1.60.
High-dimensional (d=784, K=62) FL benchmark; smallest speed-up (6x).
New cancer methylation benchmark compiled for FC unlearning.
New, highly imbalanced microbiome benchmark; used for the adversarial-removal experiments.
Clustering quality is reported as phi_f / phi*_c.
Accumulated removal time over 200-500 sequential single-point removals.
Reports per-round and average speed-up vs retraining (claimed ~84x average).
Used as the client-side unlearning step in Alg. 4.
Securely aggregates client count vectors in both training and unlearning.
Local centroids are uniformly quantized into B^d bins and flattened into the count vector q^(l).
The server samples q_j points per nonzero bin to form X_s before clustering.
Option of using bin centers weighted by counts at the server (and in the simplified Alg. 5), reducing server problem size to KL.
Clients run only K-means++ seeding; the server runs full K-means++.
Lloyd's iterations are run only at the server (T iterations), not at clients, to keep unlearning cheap.
Two-level local-then-global clustering follows divide-and-conquer distributed clustering (Guha et al. 2003; Ailon et al. 2009).
edges.evidence: App. I; remark after Lemma D.1

edges.note: Like K-FED it is one-shot, but it sends anonymized quantized counts instead of exact centroids, uses counts as weights, and supports unlearning.
Alg. 4 is claimed exact in the same sense as Lemma 5.1.
edges.evidence: Sec. 5.3: 'Alg. 4 is also an exact unlearning method'

edges.note: A single client-to-server round with an order-optimal O(log^2 K) factor for one-shot FC.
Count-weighted quantized centroids give the best loss on imbalanced TMI and Celltype.
Only the affected client may reseed and the server recomputes only on KL-scale data; other clients do nothing.
Non-iid data (K' < K) lowers the loss ratio; with K'=1 per client the bound becomes O(1) (= 2 phi*).
Exploits that seeding picks real data points by sequential D^2 sampling, so deletions matter only if a deleted point was picked.
Output is probabilistically equivalent to reseeding on X \ X_R.
Retrains with probability about RK/n and only from the first removed centroid onward.
Q-k-means relies on stability of quantized means under removal; Alg. 3 relies on removed points rarely being sampled as seeds.
Falls back to retraining only when a removed point is the first seed, otherwise doing at most a partial reseed.
Bin indices serve as RS evaluation points, nonzero counts as substitution errors, and client messages as syndromes.
The server finds the locator polynomial prod(1 - j x) from summed syndromes before factoring it to get bin indices.
Standard syndrome decoder for BCH/RS codes, reused for multiset recovery.
Uniform random keys z_i^(l) summing to zero mod p hide each client's syndromes from the server.
Aggregates sparse multisets exactly, unlike sparsification-based approximate schemes.
Masks are generated offline using standard secure model aggregation (Bonawitz et al. 2017; Bell et al. 2020; So et al. 2022).
Sends 2KL field elements instead of a B^d-length masked vector, which would be exponential in d.
The server learns only the aggregate q, not which client contributed to each bin.
Implements MUFC's privacy criterion of obfuscated client point counts.
A specialization for sparse high-dimensional vectors.
Prior schemes (Beguier 2020; Ergun 2021) have communication linear in model dimension.
Points are sampled uniformly within quantization bins (default) or placed at bin centers.
Weights enter both the D^2 sampling and the Lloyd averaging; integer weights are equivalent to point multiplicities.
Provides initial centroids for Lloyd's iterations in full K-means++.
Seeding alone gives E[phi] <= 8(ln K + 2) phi*, which is reused at clients and the server.
Clients send exact local centroids in one round.
Sends exact client centroids non-anonymously, revealing per-client statistics.
Assigns unit weights to client centroids, which hurts loss on imbalanced data (TMI 1.84).
Also uses unit centroid weights; loss 1.54 on TMI vs 1.24 for MUFC.
Clusters subsets in a computation tree whose leaves are clients in this adaptation.
Ginart et al.'s deletion-efficient exact method, used as the unlearning baseline.
Exact deletion through quantized centroids that rarely change.
Quantizes centroids after each Lloyd iteration.
Must check that the quantized centroids are unchanged at every Lloyd iteration after a removal, which drives its cost.
Costs O(nKd) per client plus server reclustering for every removal.
Trivially exact reference method.
Outliers are very likely chosen as D^2 seeds, so deleting them forces reseeding; the bound assumes P(outlier) = O(1/n).
Targeting high-cost points raises the retraining probability bound to O(RK^2 eps1 eps2 / n).
Gives an O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d) expected cost even for adversarial removals.
Expected removal time independent of dataset size n.
E[time] <= O(nKd) * P(retrain) + O(RK) with P(retrain) < O(RK/n).
Q-k-means expected removal time O(R^2 K^3 T^2 d^2.5 / eps) is much higher.
The imbalance constant eps1 = n/(K s_min) enters the adversarial bound.
The outlier parameter eps2 and the O(1/n) outlier-probability assumption are needed.
Probabilistic model equivalence to reseeding on remaining data.
The unlearned seeding keeps the 8(ln K + 2) approximation on X'.
O(log^2 K) multiplicative factor plus an O(n d gamma^2 log K) quantization term.
Composes the O(log K) factors of client and server K-means++.
The bound is stated for phi_f under induced global clustering.
Classical expected O(log K) guarantee of K-means++ seeding.
Logarithmic cost comes from sending 2KL syndromes over F_p with p >= max{n, B^d}.
Logarithmic vs linear dependence on vector dimension.
Guarantees the server's reconstruction of q is unique and exact.
Same squared-distance loss but with assignments induced via local centroids (App. L shows the difference).
The numerator is phi_f(X; C_s); the denominator approximates phi*_c by the best of several K-means++ runs.
Normalizes the K-means cost by the near-optimal centralized cost.
Clustering under the federated data-locality constraint.
An unsupervised FL problem.
A single-round variant of FC.
Centroid-based clustering objective.
Unlearning where removal requests arise at clients; prior methods (FedEraser, KD-based) lack guarantees.
This paper instantiates federated unlearning for FC, with single-client (cross-silo) and multi-client (cross-device) removal.
Unlearned model must match retraining in distribution.
Bounded difference from retraining.
The paper targets the stricter exact criterion, unlike Guo et al., Sekhari et al., and Golatkar et al.
Legal deletion rights, plus the fact that training data can be reconstructed from models.
Prevents the server from inferring client data from local models (model inversion).
FL keeps data on devices to protect privacy.
K-FED trades privacy for efficiency; Li et al. 2022 trades efficiency for privacy.
A core constraint in FL protocol design.

cross_paper.note: DC-Kmeans from Ginart et al. is adapted to the FC setting (computation tree height 2, leaves = clients) as the main unlearning baseline. MUFC gets 6-164x vs DC-KM's 2-9x speed-up under random removals. Experiment repetitions follow Ginart et al.

Appendix G contrasts Alg. 3 with Q-k-means: Q-k-means relies on quantized-mean stability and costs O(R^2 K^3 T^2 d^2.5 / eps), with no removal-time guarantee unless randomly initialized, versus O(RK^3 eps1 eps2 d) for MUFC. MUFC also borrows quantization ideas (random shifts, footnote 2) and the UK Biobank motivation.
Cited as a sharding-based exact unlearning method. MUFC achieves exactness through sampling-based seeding instead of sharding.
Both study efficient federated unlearning. MUFC targets federated K-means clustering with exact guarantees; FedShard targets supervised FL with sharding and fairness.
MFC is a multishot federated clustering approach, while MUFC is one-shot (like K-FED). MUFC's unlearning-friendly seeding and SCMA could be explored for multishot FC.
FFC adds fairness and personalization to federated clustering. Combining it with MUFC-style exact unlearning is an open direction.
